newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. let Nazis move gold via New York - report.
newsitem.headline: U.S. let Nazis move gold via New York - report.

text.p: The United States allowed Nazi Germany to transfer stolen gold worth $20 million through New York to Argentina during World War Two before clamping down on the practice, a German weekly said on Wednesday.

Die Woche said documents in the U.S. National Archive also showed Swiss banks transferred $128 million to their branches in New York in the first eight months of the war. Some of this belonged to Jewish refugees fleeing the Third Reich and some was from Nazi sources.

The U.S. froze assets moved from Germany, Switzerland and Nazi-occupied Europe on June 14, 1941, but $229 million in Jewish assets had already entered the country. One estimate suggests these frozen U.S. accounts could hold $36 billion at today's prices.

Die Woche, citing an official study of the U.S. archives due to be published next week, said U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau authorised the transfer of $20 million of French gold reserves in New York to Argentina in June 1940 after the Nazis marched into Paris.

It said previously unpublished documents in the archive showed how early the United States knew that billions of dollars worth of stolen gold from occupied Europe was passing into banks accounts in neutral countries, not just in Switzerland but also in South America via New York.

In a release ahead of publication on Thursday, the weekly said this discovery had prompted Washington to delay publishing a report on an investigation into its archives launched last October to trace gold and cash stolen by the Nazis.
"We have reached a completely new chapter in the affair," said Greg Bradsher, investigating U.S. involvement in the Nazi gold scandal at the National Archive.
Die Woche said Morgenthau knew capital was flowing into the private New York accounts of German, Swiss and Argentinian clients, but the State Department initially warned against freezing them.

"A freezing control could set off antagonism and irritation in particular European countries," it wrote in a memorandum, adding that cash and gold transferred out of Europe could be used to bargain with Germany after the war.
Morgenthau reached a compromise in June 1841 with his State Department colleagues and froze deposits from Germany, Switzerland and occupied Europe but not those from other neutral states.

He pressed for U.S. embassies, including those in Switzerland, Spain and Portugal, to gather information on Nazi gold, but was blocked by the State Department, which feared retaliation against British and U.S. prisoners in Nazi camps.
Swiss banks, after a year of arguing with Jewish groups, acknowledged in February that they held 39 million Swiss francs ($27 million) in ownerless accounts that might stem from Holocaust victims.
Both Portugal and Brazil said this week they were setting up commissions to trace cash and gold stolen by the Nazis.
